items.title: Channel sequences
proof_obligations: Use measurable input and output spaces and a probability kernel at each blocklength.
State that no consistency between different blocklengths is assumed.
items.statement: For each integer $n\ge1$, let $(\mathcal X_n,\mathcal A_n)$ and $(\mathcal Y_n,\mathcal B_n)$ be measurable spaces and let $W_n$ be a probability kernel from the first space to the second ([[def-measure-kernel-and-probability-kernel]]). The sequence $(W_n)_{n\ge1}$ is a **channel sequence**, and $n$ is its blocklength. A length-$n$ transmission sends an input in $\mathcal X_n$ and produces an output with conditional law $W_n$. No consistency between different blocklengths is assumed.

references.title: Yury Polyanskiy and Yihong Wu, Information Theory: From Coding to Learning, Chapter 19 §19.1

items.axiom_use: No choice axiom is used; this definition quantifies over supplied kernels and selects no versions.

items.title: Finite discrete memoryless channels
proof_obligations: Specify the fixed finite alphabets and single-use transition kernel.
Define every blocklength kernel by the product formula and state the memoryless convention.
items.statement:
A **finite discrete memoryless channel (DMC)** is the channel sequence [[def-channel-sequence]] with fixed finite nonempty input and output alphabets $\mathcal X,\mathcal Y$ (with every subset measurable) and one stochastic kernel $W(y\mid x)$ from $\mathcal X$ to $\mathcal Y$ ([[def-finite-stochastic-kernel]]). At every blocklength $n\ge1$ its input and output alphabets are $\mathcal X^n,\mathcal Y^n$. For a block word $a^n\in\mathcal A^n$, regarded as a function on $\{0,\ldots,n-1\}$, use the one-based coordinate labels $a_i:=a^n(i-1)$ for $1\le i\le n$. With these labels, its block kernel is
$$W^n(y^n\mid x^n):=\prod_{i=1}^n W(y_i\mid x_i).$$
Thus the same single-use transition law is applied independently at each coordinate, conditional on the input word. This page imposes no feedback or input-cost constraint.

references.title: Yury Polyanskiy and Yihong Wu, Information Theory: From Coding to Learning, Chapter 19 §19.1
Robert Gallager, Principles of Digital Communication I, Chapter 8 §8.7.1, MIT OpenCourseWare

items.axiom_use: No choice axiom is used; all alphabets and products in this definition are finite.

items.title: The DMC product laws are stochastic kernels
proof_obligations: Check nonnegativity of each product probability.
Factor the finite sum over the product output alphabet into the product of row sums.
items.statement: For a finite DMC $W$ and every $n\ge1$, the block formula $W^n(y^n\mid x^n)=\prod_{i=1}^n W(y_i\mid x_i)$ is a stochastic kernel from $\mathcal X^n$ to $\mathcal Y^n$.

references.title: Yury Polyanskiy and Yihong Wu, Information Theory: From Coding to Learning, Chapter 19 §19.1
Robert Gallager, Principles of Digital Communication I, Chapter 8 §8.7.1, MIT OpenCourseWare

items.axiom_use: No choice axiom is used; only finite products and finite sums occur.

items.title: Single-letter information capacity of a finite DMC
proof_obligations: Define the induced joint and output laws for every input probability vector.
Define capacity in nats per channel use and establish attainment on the finite input simplex.
items.statement:
For an input probability vector $P_X$ on $\mathcal X$ ([[def-finite-probability-vector]]), let $P_{XY}(x,y):=P_X(x)W(y\mid x)$ and $Q_{P_X}(y):=\sum_xP_X(x)W(y\mid x)$. Write $I(P_X;W):=I(X;Y)$ for this joint law, using [[def-it-finite-mutual-information]]. The **single-letter information capacity** is
$$C(W):=\sup_{P_X} I(P_X;W),$$
measured in nats per channel use. The finite-dimensional maximum is attained, as proved in [[lem-discrete-memoryless-channel-capacity-is-attained]].

references.title: Yury Polyanskiy and Yihong Wu, Information Theory: From Coding to Learning, Chapter 19 §§19.1–19.2
Robert Gallager, Principles of Digital Communication I, Chapter 8 §§8.7.1–8.7.2, MIT OpenCourseWare

items.axiom_use: No choice axiom is used; the input simplex and all probability laws are finite-dimensional.

items.title: Fixed-length codes for a finite DMC
proof_obligations: Specify positive blocklength, finite message set, deterministic encoder, and deterministic decoder.
State that the channel output is governed by the product DMC kernel.
items.statement: For a finite DMC $W$, a **length-$n$ code with $M$ messages** is a pair of maps $e:[M]\to\mathcal X^n$ and $d:\mathcal Y^n\to[M]$, where $n,M\ge1$ and $[M]:=\{1,\ldots,M\}$. A message $m$ is encoded as $e(m)$, passed through the block kernel $W^n$ of [[def-discrete-memoryless-channel]], and decoded as $d(Y^n)$. The encoder and decoder are deterministic; there is no feedback, and no input-cost constraint is imposed.

references.title: Yury Polyanskiy and Yihong Wu, Information Theory: From Coding to Learning, Chapter 19 §19.1
Robert Gallager, Principles of Digital Communication I, Chapter 8 §§8.7.2–8.7.3, MIT OpenCourseWare

items.axiom_use: No choice axiom is used; the message set and all code alphabets are finite.

items.title: Finite DMC information density
proof_obligations: Define the log likelihood ratio only on the support of the induced joint law.
Define its block version and zero-support convention.
items.statement:
Given an input law $P_X$, let $Q_{P_X}=P_XW$ be its output law. The **information density** is
$$\imath_{P_X}(x;y):=\ln\frac{W(y\mid x)}{Q_{P_X}(y)}$$
when $P_X(x)W(y\mid x)>0$, and is $-\infty$ otherwise. For block sequences define $\imath_{P_X}(x^n;y^n):=\sum_{i=1}^n\imath_{P_X}(x_i;y_i)$, with any sum containing $-\infty$ equal to $-\infty$. On the support of the induced joint law, both numerator and denominator are positive, and the value is finite.

references.title: Yury Polyanskiy and Yihong Wu, Information Theory: From Coding to Learning, Chapter 19 §§19.1–19.2
Robert Gallager, Principles of Digital Communication I, Chapter 8 §8.7.4, MIT OpenCourseWare

items.axiom_use: No choice axiom is used; the definition is on finite probability vectors.

items.title: Finite DMC information capacity is attained
proof_obligations: Express mutual information as output entropy minus average row entropy.
Prove continuity at zero coordinates and on the finite probability simplex.
Apply compactness and the extreme-value theorem to obtain a maximizing input law.
items.statement: For every finite DMC $W$, the supremum $C(W)$ is a maximum: there is an input probability vector $P_X^*$ such that $I(P_X^*;W)=C(W)$.

references.title: Yury Polyanskiy and Yihong Wu, Information Theory: From Coding to Learning, Chapter 19 §§19.1–19.2
Robert Gallager, Principles of Digital Communication I, Chapter 8 §8.7.2, MIT OpenCourseWare

items.axiom_use: No choice axiom is used; compactness is applied to a finite-dimensional simplex.

items.title: The n-letter mutual information of a DMC is at most nC
proof_obligations: Use the finite entropy chain rule and monotonicity under conditioning.
Use the product channel law to identify each conditional output entropy.
Bound each single-letter mutual information by C(W).
items.statement: For every input probability vector on $\mathcal X^n$ and output $Y^n$ generated by a finite DMC $W^n$, one has $I(X^n;Y^n)\le nC(W)$.

references.title: Yury Polyanskiy and Yihong Wu, Information Theory: From Coding to Learning, Chapter 19 §19.1
Robert Gallager, Principles of Digital Communication I, Chapter 8 §§8.7.2, MIT OpenCourseWare

items.axiom_use: No choice axiom is used; the random variables and all sums have finite ranges.

items.title: Average and maximal error of a fixed-length code
proof_obligations: Define conditional error for each message.
Define average error for a uniform message and maximal error without a message prior.
items.statement:
For a length-$n$ code $(e,d)$, let
$$e_m:=W^n\{y^n:d(y^n)\ne m\mid e(m)\}.$$
Its **average error** is $\varepsilon_{\rm av}:=M^{-1}\sum_{m=1}^M e_m$, corresponding to a uniform message, and its **maximal error** is $\varepsilon_{\max}:=\max_{1\le m\le M}e_m$.

references.title: Yury Polyanskiy and Yihong Wu, Information Theory: From Coding to Learning, Chapter 19 §19.1
Robert Gallager, Principles of Digital Communication I, Chapter 8 §§8.7.2–8.7.3, MIT OpenCourseWare

items.axiom_use: No choice axiom is used; errors are finite sums over messages and outputs.

items.title: IID DMC information density converges to mutual information
proof_obligations: Compute the one-letter mean from the finite mutual-information formula.
Use finite support for finite variance and prove the probability bound from the squared deviation.
items.statement: Fix a finite DMC $W$ and input law $P_X$. If $(X_i,Y_i)_{i\ge1}$ are IID with law $P_X(x)W(y\mid x)$, then $n^{-1}\imath_{P_X}(X^n;Y^n)\to I(P_X;W)$ in probability.

references.title: Yury Polyanskiy and Yihong Wu, Information Theory: From Coding to Learning, Chapter 19 §19.2
Robert Gallager, Principles of Digital Communication I, Chapter 8 §8.7.4, MIT OpenCourseWare

items.axiom_use: No choice axiom is used; the random variables have finite support.

items.title: Capacity-achieving output laws bound every row divergence
proof_obligations: Prove every output symbol reachable from an input has positive mass under a capacity-achieving output law.
Differentiate mutual information along the simplex segment toward each point mass.
Identify the one-sided derivative as D(W(·|x)||Q*)−C(W) and use maximality.
items.statement:
Let $P_X^*$ attain $C(W)$ and let $Q^*:=P_X^*W$. If $W(y\mid x)>0$, then $Q^*(y)>0$, and for every $x\in\mathcal X$,
$$D(W(\cdot\mid x)\|Q^*)\le C(W).$$

references.title: Yury Polyanskiy and Yihong Wu, Information Theory: From Coding to Learning, Chapter 19 §19.1 and Chapter 22 §22.1
MIT 6.441 Information Theory, Lecture 8, channel capacity and maximizing capacity

items.axiom_use: No choice axiom is used; the proof uses a one-dimensional path in a finite simplex.

items.title: Average-error and maximal-error DMC capacities
proof_obligations: Define rates in nats per use from message counts and blocklength.
Define reliable average-error and maximal-error rates by vanishing corresponding error.
items.statement:
A rate $R\ge0$ is **average-error achievable** for $W$ if there are length-$n$ codes for all sufficiently large $n$ with
$$\liminf_{n\to\infty}\frac{\ln M_n}{n}\ge R,\qquad \varepsilon_{\rm av}(n)\longrightarrow0.$$
It is **maximal-error achievable** if the same condition holds with $\varepsilon_{\max}(n)\to0$. Define $C_{\rm av}(W)$ and $C_{\max}(W)$ as the suprema of the respective achievable-rate sets. Rates use nats per channel use.

references.title: Yury Polyanskiy and Yihong Wu, Information Theory: From Coding to Learning, Chapter 19 §19.1
Robert Gallager, Principles of Digital Communication I, Chapter 8 §§8.7.2–8.7.3, MIT OpenCourseWare

items.axiom_use: No choice axiom is used; capacity is defined by sequences of finite codes.

items.title: Expurgation converts small average error to small maximal error
proof_obligations: Show at least half the messages have individual error no more than twice the average.
Restrict to those messages and define a decoder whose error for a retained message cannot increase.
Bound the rate loss by ln 2 divided by blocklength.
items.statement: Every length-$n$ code with average error $\varepsilon_{\rm av}$ has a subcode with at least $M/2$ messages and maximal error at most $2\varepsilon_{\rm av}$.

references.title: Yury Polyanskiy and Yihong Wu, Information Theory: From Coding to Learning, Chapter 19 §19.2
Robert Gallager, Principles of Digital Communication I, Chapter 8 §8.7.4, MIT OpenCourseWare

items.axiom_use: No choice axiom is used; the retained message set is finite.

items.title: Random coding achieves every rate below finite DMC capacity
proof_obligations: Construct an IID random codebook and unique-threshold decoder.
Bound miss probability by the IID information-density law of large numbers.
Bound each independent false alarm using E exp(i)=1, Markov's inequality, and a union bound.
Select a deterministic codebook whose average error is no greater than the ensemble mean.
items.statement: For every finite DMC $W$ and every $0\le R<C(W)$, there are fixed-length codes with $\liminf_{n\to\infty}n^{-1}\ln M_n\ge R$ and average error tending to zero.

references.title: Yury Polyanskiy and Yihong Wu, Information Theory: From Coding to Learning, Chapter 19 §19.2
Robert Gallager, Principles of Digital Communication I, Chapter 8 §8.7.4, MIT OpenCourseWare

items.axiom_use: No choice axiom is used; every random-code ensemble has finite support.

items.title: Uniform concentration around the capacity output divergence bound
proof_obligations: Bound the row-wise information-density variance uniformly over the finite input alphabet.
Use independence of channel outputs for a fixed input word and the squared-deviation tail inequality.
items.statement:
Let $P_X^*$ attain $C(W)$ and $Q^*=P_X^*W$. There is a finite constant $V\ge0$ such that, for every $n\ge1$, every $x^n\in\mathcal X^n$, and every $\delta>0$, under output law $W^n(\cdot\mid x^n)$,
$$\Pr\left[\ln\frac{W^n(Y^n\mid x^n)}{(Q^*)^n(Y^n)}>n(C(W)+\delta)\right]\le\frac{V}{n\delta^2}.$$
The likelihood ratio is evaluated only on the support of $W^n(\cdot\mid x^n)$.

references.title: Yury Polyanskiy and Yihong Wu, Information Theory: From Coding to Learning, Chapter 22 §22.1
MIT 6.441 Information Theory, Lecture 8, maximizing DMC capacity

items.axiom_use: No choice axiom is used; all alphabets and variance sums are finite.

items.title: Reliable average-error DMC rates do not exceed capacity
proof_obligations: Apply finite Fano to the uniform message and decoder output.
Show I(message; output)=I(channel input; output) for a deterministic encoder.
Apply the n-letter mutual-information bound and pass to the vanishing-error limit.
items.statement: For any sequence of fixed-length codes over a finite DMC with average errors $\varepsilon_{\rm av}(n)\to0$, one has $\limsup_{n\to\infty}n^{-1}\ln M_n\le C(W)$.

references.title: Yury Polyanskiy and Yihong Wu, Information Theory: From Coding to Learning, Chapter 17 §17.3 and Chapter 19 §19.1
Robert Gallager, Principles of Digital Communication I, Chapter 8 §8.7.3, MIT OpenCourseWare

items.axiom_use: No choice axiom is used; the message and channel alphabets are finite.

items.title: Strong converse for finite-alphabet DMCs
proof_obligations: For each decoding region, split the channel law at a log-likelihood threshold against the capacity-achieving output product law.
Use disjoint decoding regions to bound the reference-measure term by exp(threshold)/M.
Choose a threshold strictly above nC and below ln M, then use uniform concentration to show success tends to zero.
items.statement: Let $W$ be a finite DMC with finite nonempty input and output alphabets and no input-cost constraint. For any sequence of length-$n$ codes with $\liminf_{n\to\infty}n^{-1}\ln M_n>C(W)$, the average success probability tends to zero; hence both average and maximal error tend to one.

references.title: Yury Polyanskiy and Yihong Wu, Information Theory: From Coding to Learning, Chapter 22 §22.1
MIT 6.441 Information Theory, Lecture 8, maximizing capacity

items.axiom_use: No choice axiom is used; the proof uses finite decoding regions and finite probability sums.

items.title: Operational capacity formula for a finite DMC
proof_obligations: Combine the average-error converse and random-coding achievability to identify average-error capacity.
Use expurgation to identify maximal-error capacity, including the vanishing rate loss.
Use capacity attainment to replace the supremum by a maximum.
items.statement:
For every finite DMC $W$ with no input-cost constraint,
$$C_{\rm av}(W)=C_{\max}(W)=C(W)=\max_{P_X}I(P_X;W),$$
with rates and mutual information measured in nats per channel use.

references.title: Yury Polyanskiy and Yihong Wu, Information Theory: From Coding to Learning, Chapter 19 §§19.1–19.2
Robert Gallager, Principles of Digital Communication I, Chapter 8 §§8.7.2–8.7.4, MIT OpenCourseWare

items.axiom_use: No choice axiom is used; all claims concern finite-alphabet codes and distributions.

items.title: Capacity of the binary symmetric channel
proof_obligations: Compute the output law and conditional output entropy for an arbitrary Bernoulli input.
Upper-bound output entropy by ln 2 and show the uniform input attains it.
Check crossover endpoints 0, 1/2, and 1 under the 0 ln 0 convention.
items.statement:
The binary symmetric channel has input and output alphabets $\{0,1\}$; independently at each use, the output is the input bit flipped with probability $p\in[0,1]$. Write
$$h(p):=-p\ln p-(1-p)\ln(1-p),\qquad 0\ln0:=0.$$
The channel capacity is $\ln2-h(p)$ nats per use, attained by a uniform input.

references.title: MIT 6.441 Information Theory, Lecture 8, Channel Capacity and Binary Symmetric Channels
Yury Polyanskiy and Yihong Wu, Information Theory: From Coding to Learning, Chapter 19 §19.3

items.axiom_use: No choice axiom is used; all alphabets and sums are finite.

items.title: Capacity of the binary erasure channel
proof_obligations: Compute H(X|Y) by separating received-symbol and erasure outputs.
Maximize the resulting mutual information over binary input laws.
Check erasure endpoints 0 and 1.
items.statement: The binary erasure channel outputs the input bit with probability $1-\epsilon$ and the erasure symbol $e$ with probability $\epsilon$, independently at each use. For $\epsilon\in[0,1]$, its capacity is $(1-\epsilon)\ln2$ nats per use, attained by a uniform input.

references.title: MIT 6.441 Information Theory, Lecture 8, Binary Erasure Channel
Yury Polyanskiy and Yihong Wu, Information Theory: From Coding to Learning, Chapter 19 §19.3

items.axiom_use: No choice axiom is used; all alphabets and sums are finite.
